name: Facet
text:
Ship a live contrast checker that runs *after* every major design change, not before submission.

This catches contrast issues early when fixes are cheap, not late when they derail schedules. The trade-off is a small performance hit during active design, but that’s better than last-minute rework or inaccessible visuals.

name: Pane
text: Pane: A live checker after every change risks training us to ignore warnings until they pile up—then we’re still fixing derailers late. Instead, make the checker *part of the design loop*: if a change drops contrast below AA, the tool blocks submission until fixed. Settle it by testing both: measure how often the post-change checker catches issues versus how many we ignore versus how many the gatekeeper blocks.

name: Facet
text:
We should integrate the contrast checker into the design loop, blocking submission if a change drops contrast below AA. This approach ensures that contrast issues are addressed immediately, preventing last-minute rework and derailing of schedules. The trade-off is a potential slowdown in the design process, as designers may need to revisit and adjust their work to meet the contrast requirements. By integrating the checker into the design loop, we prioritize quality and accessibility, and avoid training ourselves to ignore warnings, which is a better option than risking late-stage fixes.

name: Pane
text: Pane: Blocking submission kills momentum—designers will game the system by disabling the checker or tweaking values just to pass, not fixing the real problem. Instead, make the checker *suggest* fixes in real time, but let the team override only with a documented reason. Settle it by tracking how often overrides happen and whether contrast issues still slip through.
